intro.heading: Nobody is on site, and the answer is somewhere in a folder.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: It is ten past three. A carer on a quiet night shift finds a resident who has refused their medication, or who is sitting on the floor and says they are fine. The registered manager is at home asleep. The senior is busy on another floor. The carer knows your service has a policy for this, but the paper folder is a metre of plastic wallets and the shared drive has four files with similar names. She does not want to guess, and she does not want to wake someone over something she could have looked up.

trail.text: Your care home policies are reviewed, signed off and filed.
New carers are shown where the policies are kept.
Night staff start the shift briefed and well meaning.
A carer is unsure what the policy says about the situation in front of her.
The folder is thick and the shared drive search returns six files.
She guesses, or waits for a call back, or rings someone out of hours.
Nobody knows what she did or which version she read.
An inspector asks how night staff find the right policy.

trail_close: The policies exist. Finding the right one at the right moment is the gap. Here is how a carer can ask in plain words and get an answer from your own documents, with the limits said plainly.

why.heading: A folder full of policies is not much use at 3am
why.sub: Staff do not need a perfect memory. They need a quick, reliable way to look things up.

cards.title: People ask in their own words
cards.body: A carer does not know the title of the policy she needs. She knows what is in front of her. A plain question works better than a filename.

cards.title: Search should name its source
cards.body: A carer needs to see which policy the answer came from, so she can trust it, open the full policy, and tell the manager what she relied on.

cards.title: A guess is worse than a call
cards.body: If the documents do not cover the question, the right outcome is to say so and escalate as your policy says. It must never be a confident invention.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. These are the questions we hear most.

items.q: What does a carer actually do?
items.a: She opens the Staff Hub on her phone, taps Chat, picks a topic such as Policies & Procedures and asks in plain words. She can speak the question if her browser supports it, and every answer has a Listen button that reads it aloud.

items.q: Where do the answers come from?
items.a: From the documents you uploaded, and from any knowledge entries you added by hand. The answer names the policy it used. Where we have a regulatory reference base, it can also be used as a source.

items.q: What if the policy does not cover it?
items.a: The assistant only answers when the match is close enough. Below that it says it could not find a matching policy and offers a list headed Did you mean one of these? Then she follows your escalation route.

items.q: Does it give clinical advice or replace my senior?
items.a: No. It tells the carer what your own policy says. She must still follow the policy, use her judgement and escalate to the person your policy names. If a resident is in danger, she calls for help first.

items.q: Can I see what my staff asked?
items.a: Yes. Recent queries lists who asked, when, the first question, the language and whether it matched. You can open the whole conversation. If a carer deletes a chat from her own history, the record stays for you, so tell your team that plainly.

items.q: Is it only as good as my policies?
items.a: Yes. If a policy is missing, out of date or vague, the answer will be too. A No match is useful because it points at the gap. You can also run a policy gap check.

items.q: Can I be sure it never gets it wrong?
items.a: We do not promise that. Answers are drawn from your documents and checked against a minimum match, and staff can mark an answer down. Treat it as a fast way to find your policy, not as the final word.

limits.heading: A quick way to look things up, not a substitute for judgement

cards.title: It is only as good as your uploaded policies
cards.body: It answers from your own documents. Missing, outdated or contradictory policies give weak answers, and it cannot invent a procedure you never wrote.

cards.title: It does not give clinical advice or replace a senior
cards.body: It reports what your policy says. Carers must follow the policy and escalate to the people it names. It does not call anyone, and it does not alert you to each question.

cards.title: Questions are not private from you
cards.body: Admins can see who asked what and when in Recent queries, and staff cannot erase it. Do not promise anonymity. Tell your team what you can see and why.

items.q: What is a policy assistant for care staff?
items.a: It is a chat tool that answers a carer's question from your own policies and names the policy it used. In CareStream it lives in the Staff Hub, in training built from your own policies.

items.q: Is it the same as a policy chatbot?
items.a: In everyday words, yes. It is a policy chatbot that stays inside your documents. If it cannot find a close enough match, it says so instead of guessing.

items.q: How is it different from document search on a shared drive?
items.a: Ordinary document search needs the right filename or keyword and gives back a list of files. The assistant takes a plain question and gives a short answer with the policy named, and lets her open the full policy.

items.q: Can staff do a policy search in their own language?
items.a: Yes, on the paid plans. Chat answers come back in the carer's first language and policies are translated when opened. See the multilingual Staff Hub.

items.q: Do our care home policies and procedures need to be uploaded first?
items.a: Yes. The assistant answers from what you upload, so start with the policies staff need most at night, such as medication, falls and safeguarding. Our complete guide to care home policies helps with the list.

items.q: What does the law say about staff and policies?
items.a: The regulations do not mention policies by name. Regulation 17 requires systems or processes to be established and operated effectively, and Regulation 18 requires staff to receive appropriate support and training. Easy access to your policy is one practical way to support that.

items.q: What should one care home policy cover for night staff?
items.a: Say who to call, in what order, and what to record, because a carer alone at night needs those three things. Check that your wording does not disagree with another policy, as staff follow the wrong one when it does.

items.q: What happens after the carer gets an answer?
items.a: Nothing is triggered automatically. You can see the question in Recent queries, and you can then allocate a short adhoc training module on the topic if you want to check understanding.

guide.heading: How to make your policies findable at 3am
guide.lede: A good assistant cannot rescue a policy nobody can read. These steps help whether or not you use one.

sections.h3: Write for a person standing in a corridor
paragraphs: Put the first action at the top of each policy: who to call, and what to do while waiting. Use headings that match the words carers use, such as refusing medication or found on the floor, rather than internal titles.

Under Regulation 18, staff must receive the support and training they need to do their job. A policy a carer can find and follow in a minute is part of that support, alongside your supervision and training.

sections.h3: Check your night time policies before you upload
checklist: Medication: refusals, missed doses and who to call out of hours.
Falls: what to do before moving anyone, and what to record.
Safeguarding: who to tell and how to reach them at night.
Escalation: a named person to call if the first one does not answer.

sections.h3: Tell your team what you can see
paragraphs: Explain that Recent queries shows who asked what. Say you use it to fix policies and support staff, not to catch anyone out. People ask more honest questions when they know the rules.

guide.note: For the inspector. Be ready to show where staff find policies out of hours, and what you changed when a question found no match. See the Care Quality Commission for its own guidance.
